title: Maintaining
hook: keeping good states going and growing

segments.voice: Yesterday: arousing, bringing a good quality into being. Wake the good, starting small.

Day one of a new habit has the thrill of starting. Day two is just doing it again. No fanfare, no new pen. A beautiful journal gets three lovely pages, and six months later it turns up under the bed, the rest of it blank. Starting a good thing is the third effort. Keeping it going is the fourth, and for this one the Buddha reached for pictures from the farmyard and the workshop.
screen: `DAY ONE: THE THRILL.` → `DAY TWO: AGAIN.` → `THE JOURNAL UNDER THE BED.`

segments.voice: The fourth effort, in the Numbered Discourses, is for wholesome states already arisen: you work to keep them, so they don't fade or get muddled, and help them grow to fullness. The Pali name is anurakkhaṇā, protecting, guarding what you have. The list's own example is a meditator protecting a steady object of concentration once they've found it. But how do you keep at something without straining? A sutta in the Connected Discourses gives two pictures. A hen sits on her eggs, eight or ten or twelve, covering them, warming them, tending them properly. She doesn't need to wish, may my chicks break out today. If she keeps sitting, they will. Then a carpenter looks at the handle of his adze, a woodworking tool, and sees the marks his fingers have worn into it. He couldn't say how much wore away today, or yesterday. But it wore. Just so, the Buddha says, a monk can't see how much of the mind's taints wore away today, but steady practice wears them away. The Dhammapada adds the other half, in Max Müller's words: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good." Gladness isn't a distraction from keeping a good thing going. It's part of what keeps it going.
screen: `ANURAKKHAṆĀ: GUARDING WHAT'S GROWN.` · `THE HEN ON HER EGGS.` · `THE WORN ADZE HANDLE.` · `DO IT AGAIN, AND ENJOY IT.` · then, large: `KEEP IT GOING.`

segments.voice: Bring back any good thing you've been doing lately, without measuring it or asking whether it's working. Picture yourself doing it again, the way a hen settles back onto her eggs, no fuss, no wishing, and let a little gladness come with the picture if it wants to.
Maintaining. Anurakkhaṇā, the fourth effort: keeping good states going and growing, like a hen sitting on her eggs.
Your line: keep it going. The hen just keeps sitting, and in time the chicks break out. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners keep daily routines, a morning sit, evening chanting, regular offerings, and many traditions encourage rejoicing in one's own good deeds as a way of sustaining them.

chat.says: How do you keep a good habit going without burning out?
options: Like a hen on her eggs: keep returning, no fuss, and enjoy doing good again.
Check every day whether it's working, and quit if you can't see change.
Push harder each week; gladness only distracts from real practice.
chat.meaning: The hen keeps sitting without wishing, and the adze handle wears away unseen. Dhammapada 118: do good again, and delight in it.

anurakkhaṇā.meaning: protecting, guarding the good that has grown

adze.meaning: a carpenter's woodworking tool with a handle

Connected Discourses.meaning: the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's teachings grouped by topic

Dhammapada.meaning: a short, much-loved collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: removed sweeping hook claims ('day two of anything is harder', 'every gym knows') and the superlative 'most patient pictures'; the adze-handle simile now says what wears away in SN 22.101 (the taints, āsavas), which the earlier line left vague.
Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 118 in SBE 10.
SN 22.101 paraphrased (hen with eight, ten or twelve eggs; carpenter's adze handle). The same hen simile also appears in MN 16 and AN 7.71. Confirm numbering.
AN 4.14's example for anurakkhaṇā (guarding an arisen concentration sign, e.g. the perception of a skeleton) is summarized without the specific perceptions.
